headlines.article_text: Jim Cramer: Apple, AMD, jobs report in week ahead Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CNBC’s Jim Cramer warned that Wall Street could face more volatility next week as concerns about AI spending continue to weigh on technology stocks. Investors await earnings from Apple, AMD, and other major companies, as well as the midterm elections and the monthly jobs report. CNBC's Jim Cramer warned on Friday that volatility on Wall Street may not be over. Stocks endured a turbulent week as renewed concerns about the artificial intelligence trade weighed on technology shares. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.3% through Wednesday before plunging 2.9% Friday, ending the week down 2%. The S&P 500 followed a similar pattern, rising 1.6% through Wednesday before tumbling 1.8% Friday to finish the week down 0.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average also reversed course, gaining 0.5% through Wednesday before slipping 1.1% Friday to end the week down 0.9%. "After a brutal week for tech, don't assume the worst is behind us," the " Mad Money " host said. "We've got the election, uncertainty overseas, the jobs report and another slew of earnings." "My advice?" he added. "Don't try to call the bottom in the Nasdaq just yet. Pick up some high-quality companies that are being thrown away, and remember, in this market, even great earnings might not be enough to send a stock higher." With that backdrop, Cramer turned to the week ahead. Monday Apple reports after the bell. Shares recently hit an all-time high, helped by enthusiasm for its latest products, including the upcoming Duo foldable phone. Cramer remains bullish on the company but acknowledged that its valuation of almost 40 times earnings leaves little room for disappointment. "You can trade it, but I am going to own it," he said. Cramer also expects encouraging results from Palantir when it reports, citing strong customer feedback about the value of its AI software. Tuesday The midterm elections take center stage, with Cramer watching whether a shift in congressional control could threaten planned data center projects. He warned that growing political opposition to the facilities could delay construction and hurt companies whose growth depends heavily on AI infrastructure spending. However, he's "not going to write off the data center entirely because there are plenty of states that will welcome them." On the earnings front, Advanced Micro Devices reports, offering another important test for the semiconductor sector following Intel's disappointing results . Cramer expects AMD to report better numbers than rival Intel. Drugmakers Pfizer and Amgen also report. Cramer said both could benefit from renewed investor enthusiasm for pharmaceutical stocks. Wednesday CVS Health reports, and Cramer remains intrigued by the company's position in the healthcare sector. However, he expressed concerns about its pharmacy benefit management business. "I wish it could disengage with that business; its stock would go higher," he said. McDonald's earnings will also be in focus. Cramer wants to see whether the company's restaurant improvement strategy is gaining traction amid reported concerns from franchisees. Thursday Kimberly-Clark reports, with Cramer optimistic about the consumer products company's prospects following its planned merger with Kenvue . The stock has benefited from investors rotating into consumer staples, and Cramer remains bullish on the company. "If this one falls before then, I think you should pick some up," he said. Friday The monthly jobs report will provide another important test for markets. Cramer expects strong hiring but limited wage growth, a combination that could help ease inflation concerns and explain the relative stability in Treasury yields. The CNBC Investing Club will also hold its annual meeting, where Cramer and Jeff Marks will discuss the portfolio, market risks and their biggest investment winners. headlines.article_text: Amazon, Intel shares fall after earnings amid AI spending concerns Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Intel shares fell 29% on Friday, posting the stock's worst day since the 1970s. The chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance, citing ongoing softness in the PC market. Amazon also sold off following an earnings miss. In this article AMZN INTC Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan speaks during a keynote presentation at Computex in Taipei on June 2, 2026. Cheng Yu-chen | Afp | Getty Images Intel shares plummeted 29% on Friday, their worst day since the 1970s, after the chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance due to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing softness in the PC market. It's a major setback for CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, and has since been on a campaign to revive the company after it missed out on the early years of the artificial intelligence boom. Intel's plunge is also a big hit to the Trump administration, which led the U.S. government into taking a 10% stake in the company over a year ago. While it's still a profitable investment, the value of those holdings dropped by about $12 billion on Friday. Nvidia also took a big stake in Intel, and its stock dropped by about $6 billion in value. Heading into Thursday's earnings report, Intel shares were up about 150% this year, buoyed by demand for central processors, which are becoming critical to agentic AI workloads. Analysts at D.A. Davidson downgraded the stock to neutral from buy on Friday in a report titled, "Not fixed yet." "We understand the PC market is being impacted at the industry level," the analysts wrote. "However it is hard to justify the current multiple when weakness is so significant." Amazon and Intel stock chart Amazon shares also sold off on Friday, slipping 1.4%, after the company reported a third-quarter miss on the top and bottom line while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, and a big increase from the previous period. The Nasdaq Composite slid 2.9%, capping off a week of rough tech earnings. Alphabet on Thursday suffered its worst day on record, plunging more than 12%. The stock fell again on Friday. Other semiconductor names also notched declines. Chip giant Nvidia fell 4%, while Broadcom dropped more than 5% and mobile chipmaker Qualcomm tumbled 11%. Not a 'moment of reckoning' Investors are growing nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether their investments will pay off. "I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday. For Intel, the disappointing forecast reflects a PC market that's getting hammered due to soaring costs for memory and other components. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research . Read more CNBC tech news AI build-out hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecasts Trump tech allies swap AI for 'super intelligence' in earnings calls Tech giants need legacy businesses to keep growing as they pour trillions into the AI buildout Nvidia responds to accusations that Jensen Huang was Chinese target Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents this quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG. "We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth." The guidance also accounts for the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said. Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips. Key to Tan's turnaround effort is Intel's foundry business, which has struggled to find its footing. Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . Its next Arizona fab is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028. Intel still has no external customers for its new chips. "We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips.
